title: Unhappiness: choice or circumstance?
description: This article explores the idea that true happiness depends less on external circumstances and more on internal perception and personal choices. It highlights how clinging to high expectations makes us vulnerable to dissatisfaction, whereas accepting reality and practicing gratitude foster more resilient happiness. The core idea is that recognizing your responsibility for your own internal state is the key to a more fulfilling and satisfied life.

texts: It might seem like an absurd question. How can you choose to be unhappy? After all, we all want to be happy, but sometimes we shift the responsibility for our well-being onto circumstances, other people, fate, or our problems.
If you’ve noticed yourself having these thoughts:
• I’m destined to be unhappy;
• I’ll only be able to live a good life when I don’t have any problems;
• My happiness depends on what happens to me;
• Others are luckier than me: they have the chance to live well, but I don’t.
This means you’re caught in a belief that joy and self-confidence depend on external factors.
This leaves you vulnerable, as the world around you is often beyond your control, making your mood a hostage to external circumstances.
<q author="Confucius">Happiness is not having everything, but making the best of everything you have.</q>
Such beliefs imply that you need every desired thing and perfect conditions, and that you must be shielded from all troubles; otherwise, life will become unbearable and you’ll never be happy.
They are based on the mistaken assumption that happiness depends solely on external factors and the absence of problems.
Clinging to this belief makes you vulnerable to dissatisfaction and despair when life fails to meet your high expectations.

<important>True happiness doesn’t depend solely on material wealth or a carefree life. It stems from our ability to adapt, find joy in the little things, and show resilience in the face of adversity.</important>
About 50% of life satisfaction depends on personality traits. Some people are simply never satisfied.
Life satisfaction depends on external circumstances by only 10–15%, while 35–40% is shaped by our decisions and choices. Therefore, one of life’s most important tasks is learning how to be happy.
Modern psychological research shows that the source of happiness lies not so much in external factors as within ourselves. High expectations can negatively impact our well-being.
People with high expectations often strive for perfection and constantly feel the pressure of having to meet high standards.

While high expectations can motivate us to achieve goals, if they become excessive and unrealistic, they can lead to stress, anxiety, and unhappiness. Constantly expecting more than what is actually present leads to disappointment and a negative perception of life.
<q author="Roy Bennett">If you are not grateful for what you already have, you will feel that you would be happier if you had much more.</q>
The happiness paradox: fewer expectations — more joy.
Research shows that the fewer expectations we have of life and the less we strive for perfection, the more likely we are to be happy. This is due to several factors:
• Accepting reality. When we stop idealizing our lives, we begin to accept them as they are. This allows us to enjoy the present rather than waiting for happiness in the future.
• Reducing stress. High expectations create constant stress and anxiety. By re-evaluating our expectations and accepting that not everything has to be perfect, we release unnecessary tension.

• Gratitude. One way to find happiness in a world of high expectations is through a gratitude practice. When we learn to appreciate what we have, even if it doesn’t meet our high expectations, we feel happier and more satisfied.
It’s important to be honest with yourself: do you see yourself as the author of your own life or as a victim of circumstances? Do you feel in control of your life, or do things just happen to you?
Consider these differences:
• Do you think for yourself, or do others think for you?
• Do you take action, or do you just follow others’ instructions?
• Are you living life to the fullest, or are you just existing?
An author of their own life takes responsibility for their actions and understands that they shape their own experiences.
Life is shaped by decisions, and everything we have—or don’t have—is the result of our own choices.
An author thinks from an “I” position: I am ready, I did it, I plan, I want, I can, I decided (they independently choose the direction of their life).
A victim is the complete opposite. Such a person believes that everything happens to them against their will.
Common phrases of a victim include: “I have to,” “I’m forced to,” “I must,” “it just happened,” “it’s because of them” (they act under the influence of circumstances or other people).

<important>Unfortunately, society often benefits from raising victims, as they are easier to manipulate. This is why many people get used to being victims, shaped by traditional models of education and upbringing.</important>
But there is good news: being a victim is just a thinking habit—an unhelpful belief that can be changed.
Real-life examples show that changing our perception of the world can lead to positive changes and increase life satisfaction.
Our attitude toward events, our ability to accept ourselves, manage our emotions, and reflect on our values all play a key role in creating happiness.
Realizing that our happiness largely depends on us gives us a powerful tool to improve our mental well-being.
Changing your inner world and perception can be the key to a happier, more fulfilling life, even in difficult and challenging circumstances.

exercise.title: How to stop being a victim and take responsibility for your happiness?
exercise.description: This article encourages you to let go of a victim mindset and take charge of your life by managing your thoughts and actions. It suggests using journaling to identify unhelpful beliefs and developing a proactive mindset through targeted questioning. Moving toward an active role in life requires patience, mindfulness, and the gradual achievement of realistic goals.

texts: The belief that “I am a victim of circumstances” is based on the idea that external factors—such as your life situation, relationships, age, finances, health, or other circumstances—limit your opportunities and prevent you from living a full and happy life.
While circumstances can indeed be unfavorable, we are fully responsible for our own lives and mental well-being.

<important>“Happiness depends not on external circumstances, but on how we perceive them.” This phrase might sound cliché, but it holds a profound truth that can change your entire perspective on happiness and how to achieve it.</important>
The first step toward breaking the cycle of self-victimization and blaming the world is realizing that these thoughts are not only unhelpful, but also emotionally exhausting.
Start journaling
Write down your thoughts, emotions, and actions. You can use an automatic thought journal or a more free-form style of recording.

Note the moments when you feel like a victim, and record the specific situations and the reasons behind them. For example: “When my colleague got a promotion and I didn’t, I felt like a victim of the system.”
Record the thoughts and beliefs that reinforce this state. For example: “I believe I can’t change my life” or “I don’t deserve success.”
Ask yourself questions to gain a deeper understanding of the beliefs and situations that support your victim role:
• Why do I feel like a victim in this situation?
• What emotions am I experiencing?
• Which events or situations reinforce my role as a victim?
• How do these thoughts and beliefs affect my life?
• How can I change my thoughts and beliefs?
Taking responsibility
Once you’ve identified your behavioral patterns, make the decision to take responsibility for your life.
Acknowledge that you control your reactions and actions, regardless of the circumstances.
Realize that you are not a victim of fate or other people, and that you have the power to change your situation.
Write a short essay expressing your commitment to taking responsibility. For example:
• I realize that only I can influence my life and its outcomes.
• I take responsibility for my thoughts, emotions, and actions.
• I understand that I have a choice in how I view situations and how I respond to them.
• I am letting go of a victim mindset and will actively seek opportunities for personal growth.
Moving from passive to active
Instead of remaining a passive observer, take an active role in your life.
• Write down your goals and desires.
• Develop an action plan to achieve them.
• Don’t be afraid to take initiative and move toward your desired results.
Example list of goals and desires:
Health:
• Start exercising regularly; join a gym.
• Improve my diet by adding more fresh fruits and vegetables.
Career and Education:
• Set a goal to improve my qualifications, learn new skills, or pursue further education in my field.
• Develop a career growth plan and define a goal, such as reaching a specific position or role.
Personal Relationships and Self-Development:
• Try to be more empathetic and attentive to the needs of others.
• Develop conflict management skills and learn to set healthy boundaries in relationships.
Write these goals and desires in a visible place and start creating specific action plans to achieve them.
Remember that your goals should be realistic, measurable, and achievable. Set deadlines and move toward them step by step.
Learn to monitor your speech
Replace questions that express complaints with questions that prompt action. This will help you develop personal responsibility and move away from a victim mindset.

Avoid questions that start with “why.” Questions like “Why does nobody love me?”, “Why doesn’t anyone want to work?”, or “Why did this happen to me?” are unproductive because they don’t lead to solutions.
These questions only reinforce the feeling that you are a victim of circumstances and that you don’t believe in your ability to change anything.
Use questions that start with “what” and “how.” These questions encourage action and foster proactive thinking.
The question “Why is this happening to me?” doesn’t require an answer—it’s more of a complaint.
The question “Why did this happen?” helps you understand the causes and find ways to improve.
Limit the use of rhetorical questions
Rhetorical questions that don’t expect an answer can reinforce a victim mindset.
Try to avoid them and focus on questions that encourage you to seek solutions and take responsibility for your life.
Be patient
Moving away from a victim mindset is a process that takes time and effort.
It’s impossible to change your thinking and behavior instantly.
Be patient and practice mindfulness to recognize situations where victimhood manifests.
As you develop patience, you create the opportunity to respond to situations more mindfully and choose more adaptive patterns of behavior.
Remember that change requires time and practice.
Be kind to yourself, keep putting in the effort, and over time, you will be able to overcome a victim mindset and take charge of your life.
<q author="Dalai Lama">Happiness is not something ready-made. It comes from your own actions.</q>
